prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock first after reading all eight ballots. Seven of eight members rank it, four place it in their top three, and nobody argues against it on scientific grounds. What persuades me is the combination of a clean physical idea and quantitative control. Katori's magic-wavelength condition makes the light shift of the clock transition cancel, so atoms can be held in a lattice without being perturbed. That removed the old trade-off between the number of atoms, which gives stability, and the perturbation of the transition, which limits accuracy. Ye's group then turned the idea into a measurement of the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-sized sample and into a controlled many-body clock. Several independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) now reproduce and compare clocks at the 10^-18 level, and the interpretation is stable. The prize would reward a real two-person lineage, an idea and its realisation, with no need to pretend that a collaboration is a person. It also fits what I think the physics prize is for: a new quantitative window on nature, here relativity, constants and the second, whose uses nobody could foresee when the first lattice clock was proposed.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap and attribution. The frequency comb was recognised in 2005 and Wineland's ion-trap work in 2012, so some colleagues will see this as a further step in precision rather than a new discovery. A Nobel prize for a record uncertainty also invites the question of why Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the Yb and Al+ clock communities are not credited. I cannot dismiss this. My answer is that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct concept, not a refinement of either earlier prize, and that the citation should name the invention and its realisation rather than the precision record alone. I also admit that I have not settled in my own mind how to weigh Katori's idea against the performance records from Ye's group, and a citation worded as a pure record would be the weak point.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube neutrino astronomy first as a new observational window that fits the committee tradition, and puts the optical clocks only sixth because of overlap with the frequency-comb prize and doubts about the 10^-18 priority claims.
responses.response: I agree that IceCube opened a genuine new window and I take the discovery seriously, but my reservation is attribution and maturity, not worth. Your own ballot says that Baikal, DUMAND and AMANDA pioneers and the wider collaboration complicate a two-name award, and Mehlig and Olsson both note that source identification is still partial. On the clocks, I do not think the comb prize covers them. Hall and Hänsch gave the ruler for optical frequencies. Katori's magic-wavelength idea is what made neutral atoms in a lattice a usable reference at all, and the 10^-18 level has been reached and compared in several laboratories, which answers the priority worry in your uncertainties. I would put the clocks above IceCube for that reason, though I would not object strongly if the committee wanted astroparticle physics this year.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks twisted bilayer graphene first because a simple, analysable continuum model predicted the flat band and experiment then found correlated insulators and superconductivity; he considers the field mature enough despite the open pairing mechanism.
responses.response: I respect the theory-experiment pairing, and I am attracted by a model that can be analysed on paper, since I work with such models myself. Where we differ is on timing. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved, and Pearce and Johansson both call the recognition a little early. The 2018 experiments are about eight years old. The clocks have an interpretation that has not changed in a decade and agreement between laboratories at the 10^-18 level. Condensed matter is not my field, so I defer to you on whether the Bistritzer-MacDonald theory alone is already decisive. If the committee prefers a moiré prize, I would want the citation to say what is established, correlated phases and superconductivity in a tunable flat band, and not the mechanism.

responses.point: Kroll shares the first place for optical lattice clocks, valuing the clear performance metrics, the road to redefining the second and the independent confirmation, but flags allocation against other clock groups (Yb lattice, Al+ ions) and says he has not verified the magic-wavelength priority claims.
responses.response: We agree on the ranking, and your caution about Lemonde, Ludlow and the Yb and Al+ groups is fair; I think it is the main objection we must answer. I would handle it in the citation, crediting the lattice-clock concept and its realisation, which leaves the ion-clock work and the metrological comparisons as part of the field and not the claim. On priority I would ask for an expert check of the 2001-03 magic-wavelength proposals before we finalise, since neither of us has the papers in front of us. Where I differ slightly is your emphasis on geodesy and applications. I would rather cite the tests of relativity and the control of many-body effects than a technological promise.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and cold atoms in optical lattices second, arguing that circuit QED is the clean path from basic physics to an enabling platform, and says his closeness to the field may bias him.
responses.response: I appreciate that you declared your connection to circuit QED. Scientifically I agree that strong coupling on a chip is elegant, and I ranked it sixth, but I am cautious for two reasons you partly raise yourself. The 2025 prize already recognised circuit quantum behaviour, and the credited names leave out Wallraff, whose first strong-coupling experiment you call arguably decisive. A prize that omits him cannot be called complete. I share your second place for the optical-lattice work, which is the one I would name as an alternative, but I think your trio of Bloch, Greiner and Zoller leaves out Esslinger and Cirac with real claims, as you say, so that case needs more resolution than the clocks.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a new invention distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-trap recognitions.
How to word a citation that credits the concept and its realisation without crediting only the precision record, and whether an expert check of the magic-wavelength priority is needed.
If the committee prefers a cold-atom prize, which three of Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Zoller and Cirac would be chosen is unresolved.
I cannot judge the condensed-matter and astroparticle cases at the level of detail that Mehlig, Eriksson and Danielsson can, so my view of their timing relies on their statements.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with the shortlisted candidates is apparent from the provided profile: Katori, Ye and the other credited names are not among my listed collaborators. I am a close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and work in atomic, molecular and optical physics, which is near the clock and cold-atom candidates, but I do not see that as a reason to recuse.
